title: Pierre and Marie Curie: A Marriage of Equals
text:
Maria Sklodowska came from Warsaw to Paris in 1891 to study physics, living on very little in a cold attic room. In 1894 she met Pierre Curie, a physicist already known for his work on crystals and magnetism. They married in July 1895. Instead of a wedding dress she wore a dark blue outfit she could use in the laboratory, and they spent their honeymoon touring France by bicycle.

For her doctoral research Marie chose the strange rays given off by uranium, discovered by Henri Becquerel. She found that the ore pitchblende was more active than its uranium could explain. Pierre put his own research aside to join her. In 1898 they announced two new elements, polonium, named after her homeland, and radium. To isolate radium they processed tons of pitchblende residue in a leaky shed at the School of Physics and Chemistry, Marie stirring boiling masses with an iron rod.

In 1903 the Nobel Committee at first planned to honor only Pierre and Becquerel. Pierre insisted that Marie be included, and the three shared the Physics prize. Three years later, in April 1906, Pierre was killed by a horse-drawn wagon on a Paris street. Marie took over his professorship at the Sorbonne, the first woman to teach there, and won a second Nobel Prize, in chemistry, in 1911. Their daughter Irene later won one too.
lesson: A partnership works best when each person's ability is fully recognized. Standing up for a partner's share of the credit is part of the work, not a favor.
source: Marie Curie, Pierre Curie (1923); Eve Curie, Madame Curie (1937)
